title: “I’ve Seen How This Goes”: Characterizing the Diversity of LLM Generations and Human Writing via Progressive Conditional Surprise

paper.title: “I’ve Seen How This Goes”: Characterizing the Diversity of LLM Generations and Human Writing via Progressive Conditional Surprise
paper.abstract:
Abstract Measuring the diversity of creative outputs is central to evaluating post-training mode collapse, comparing decoding strategies, and quantifying creative behavior in both AI and human writing.
We propose a new approach to measuring diversity using in-context learning, of which the “Decan” metric, D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} , is the working instance we evaluate: a per-byte score read off the per-token log-probabilities of a base model θ \theta in a single forward pass per permutation, with no embedding model, no reference corpus, and no human labels.
This approach is grounded in information theory, makes use of language model in-context learning to detect a wide range of similarities between any number of inputs, and obviates the need to train a special-purpose model.
The same pipeline scores AI samples and human-written response sets, with diversity treated as a property of (responses, prompt, scoring model).
On Tevet and Berant’s human-grounded McDiv benchmark, D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} reaches OCA 0.846 on the McDiv prompt_gen set where it performs best, behind the strongest neural baseline reported in Tevet and Berant (SentBERT, 0.897).
On the OLMo-2-7B post-training pipeline, D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} drops monotonically across the base → \to SFT → \to DPO → \to RLVR stages, detecting the type of diversity loss that creative-writing applications care about.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: This section defines the three quantities used in the main body: the progressive conditional surprise curve a k a_{k} , the coherence term C C , and the scalar score D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} . The full information-theoretic motivation, the alternative excess-entropy summary E E , and the cross-mode learning analysis appear in Appendices D – G .

sections.heading: 3.1 Progressive Conditional Surprise
sections.text: Given prompt p p and n n responses r 1 , … , r n r_{1},\ldots,r_{n} from policy π \pi , define a k = − log 2 ⁡ θ ⁡ ( r k ∣ r < k , p ) for ​ k = 1 , … , n , a_{k}=-\log_{2}\theta(r_{k}\mid r_{<k},p)\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,n, (3) the total surprise of the k k -th response under base model θ \theta given the previous k − 1 k{-}1 responses. The sequence ( a 1 , … , a n ) (a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}) is the progressive conditional surprise curve . We normalize each a k a_{k} by the byte count ‖ r k ‖ \|r_{k}\| to get a per-byte (bits/byte) curve that is independent of θ \theta ’s tokenizer. All quantities below are per-byte unless otherwise stated. The intuition is that as θ \theta sees more responses from π \pi , the conditional surprise drops if the responses share patterns ( θ \theta ’s in-context learning picks up on modes, stylistic regularities, topic patterns) and stays flat if they do not. For a policy with rich coherent diversity the curve declines and levels off at a positive floor; for a policy producing one repeated mode the curve drops sharply to near zero; for pure noise the curve stays roughly constant at a high value. In practice we average a k a_{k} over uniformly random permutations of the response ordering (so each position averages over all responses and the curve reflects only how θ \theta ’s predictions improve with more context, not which response happened to land in slot k k ). We take the metric value to be the last observed point a n a_{n} . Equivalently, a n = H θ ​ ( r n ∣ p ) − I θ ​ ( r n ; r 1 , … , r n − 1 ∣ p ) a_{n}=H_{\theta}(r_{n}\mid p)-I_{\theta}(r_{n};r_{1},\ldots,r_{n-1}\mid p) : the response’s individual surprise under θ \theta minus how much the prior responses make it predictable. High a n a_{n} therefore requires r n r_{n} to be both individually surprising and not made predictable by the others, two properties one would want a diversity score to reward. No fitting or extrapolation step is involved. The curve a k a_{k} is itself informative: its shape distinguishes a one-mode collapse (sharp drop to a low floor) from richer diversity (gradual decline to a higher floor) in ways the endpoint alone obscures.

sections.text: The curve alone is fooled by pure noise: θ \theta can never predict random tokens from one another, so a n a_{n} stays at the high unconditional surprise level and noise would dominate the metric. sections.heading: Sampling diversity metrics.
sections.text: Work on decoding-time diversity typically operates at the surface level: n n -gram overlap ( Li et al., 2016 ) and self-BLEU ( Zhu et al., 2018 ) . Our approach operates at the distributional level and can distinguish policies that produce lexically varied but semantically redundant outputs.

sections.heading: Diversity evaluation benchmarks.
sections.text: Tevet & Berant (2021) introduced a systematic framework for evaluating diversity metrics, with their McDiv benchmark providing human-labeled response sets at two diversity levels. We use McDiv for validation (Section 5 ), though we identify a construction confound in how its low-diversity sets are produced (Appendix E ). More recent work has revisited the meta-evaluation problem. NoveltyBench ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) defines diversity through pairwise functional equivalence rather than binary labels, training a DeBERTa classifier to group generations into equivalence classes and computing a Distinct k score (the number of meaningfully different outputs in k k samples), conceptually close to our mode count. However, their ground truth is itself a trained classifier (79% accuracy), making it unclear whether correlation with their labels validates a metric or merely measures agreement between two model-based scores. Zhang et al. (2025b) conduct a meta-evaluation of diversity metrics for constrained commonsense generation, using GPT-4o as an annotator in place of crowd workers. Guo et al. (2024) benchmark linguistic diversity of LLMs, building on Tevet and Berant’s framework with a broader set of generation tasks.

sections.heading: Perplexity.
sections.text: The coherence term C = 1 / PPL C=1/\mathrm{PPL} (Section 3.2 ) connects our framework to the standard language modeling evaluation metric. The primary diversity score D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} operates in bits/byte, weighting the residual surprise floor by output plausibility.

sections.heading: Coherence as a signal.
sections.text: Our coherence term C C uses the base model’s predictive distribution as an unsupervised quality signal. This connects to a broader line of work using model-internal coherence without external supervision: Qiu et al. (2026) show theoretically that feedback-free self-improvement methods work by optimizing coherence (compressibility of context-to-behavior mappings), and Wen et al. (2025) use internal coherence maximization to elicit capabilities from language models. Our framework leverages a related insight: the base model’s ability to compress responses in context provides a meaningful signal about their diversity structure.

sections.heading: Embedding-based diversity.
sections.text: Du & Black (2019) introduced the embedding-based approach, clustering sentence embeddings of generated responses with k k -means and reporting cluster inertia as the diversity score; subsequent work has explored alternative geometric statistics over embedded responses. These approaches are complementary to ours: they capture semantic distance in a learned representation space, while our metric captures statistical independence under a generative model. The approaches may disagree when θ \theta ’s in-context learning captures structure invisible to the embedding model, or vice versa.

sections.heading: Output collapse in RL training.
sections.text: Wang et al. (2025) document an “Echo Trap” pattern during multi-turn agent RL: early-stage agents produce varied symbolic reasoning, then collapse to deterministic templates as training proceeds. They detect this collapse using within-prompt reward standard deviation as an early-warning signal, a proxy that relies on the reward distinguishing degenerate outputs from diverse ones. The a k a_{k} framework provides a text-level alternative: collapse should appear as a drop in a n a_{n} on the agent’s own outputs, independent of reward structure. A downside of using the a k a_{k} framework is that it is unconnected from a downstream task. Responses can both be "diverse" as measured by a k a_{k} -based metrics and fail uniformly.

sections.heading: Excess entropy.
sections.text: The a k a_{k} curve also admits an excess-entropy summary related to the computational mechanics literature ( Crutchfield & Feldman, 2003 ) ; see Appendix D . We found it empirically inferior to D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} on Tevet and Berant’s diversity-eval benchmark ( Tevet & Berant, 2021 ) .

sections.heading: 5 Tevet–Berant Diversity-Eval: Human-Grounded Validation
sections.text: A diversity metric should be tested against human judgements on a standardized eval; Tevet & Berant (2021) provide both. Their McDiv and ConTest datasets pair human-grounded diversity labels with a fixed comparison protocol (Spearman ρ \rho and OCA: optimal classification accuracy , the best accuracy achievable by a one-dimensional threshold separating low- and high-diversity sets), the standard methodology for ranking diversity metrics against human judgements. The response sets are written by Mechanical Turk workers, and for both McDiv_nuggets and ConTest the high/low label is fixed by the construction protocol itself: a worker writes five different continuations (the high-diversity set), then self-selects one of those continuations and paraphrases it five times preserving content but varying form (the low-diversity set; see Appendix E for the full protocol and a construction-confound caveat). We run D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} through this evaluation pipeline.

sections.heading: Headline result.
sections.text: On the binary tasks D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} clearly tracks diversity, with OCA between 3.7% and 21.0% behind SentBERT (Table 2 ). On McDiv prompt_gen, where D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} performs best, it reaches ρ = + 0.729 \rho=+0.729{} and OCA = 0.846, against SentBERT’s ρ = + 0.796 \rho=+0.796{} and OCA = 0.897; the corresponding ROC AUC is 0.921. The headline takeaway is that an ICL-based diversity metric reaches close to a sentence-embedding baseline on a human-grounded eval, with no embedding model, no reference corpus, and no human labels in the metric itself.

(2024) ’s finding that the relationship between sampling temperature and creativity is more nuanced and weaker than the “creativity parameter” framing suggests. sections.heading: Caveats.
sections.text: The McDiv_nuggets construction protocol introduces a confound: low-diversity sets are paraphrases of specific, dramatic endings that are intrinsically more surprising to the base model than typical high-diversity continuations. Appendix E documents the mechanism, the per-byte a 1 a_{1} gap, and an evidence-by-length-bin breakdown showing the effect is content-driven not length-driven. The C C weighting in D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} helps on this benchmark partly for that confound-related reason; on settings without such a confound we expect a n a_{n} to carry most of the signal.

sections.heading: 6 OLMo-2-7B Post-Training: AI-Side Validation
sections.text: The Tevet evaluation in Section 5 validates D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} against human-grounded labels. This section evaluates D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} on real policies: we sample from four post-training stages of the same base model and ask whether the metric detects the diversity loss widely attributed to RLHF ( Kirk et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Padmakumar & He, 2023 ) . The same scoring pipeline applies to both human-written response sets (Section 5 ) and the policy-sampled sets here, so θ \theta is held fixed across the two evaluations.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We sample from the four released stages of the OLMo-2-1124-7B pipeline ( OLMo et al., 2024 ) : the pretrained base model, its SFT checkpoint, the DPO checkpoint trained on preference data, and the final RLVR-tuned Instruct checkpoint. On two prompt sets, 200 AlpacaFarm evaluation prompts ( Dubois et al., 2023 ) (seed=42 subsample of the 805-prompt set later adopted by AlpacaEval) and 100 curated NoveltyBench prompts ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) , we draw K = 10 K{=}10 responses per prompt per stage (temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, max_new_tokens = 100 \texttt{max\_new\_tokens}{=}100 ). Base runs raw; SFT / DPO / Instruct receive the prompt through their own chat template. Because per-byte cross-entropy in a causal LM decreases with within-response context, we truncate every (stage, prompt) tuple’s responses to a common per-prompt UTF-8 byte length before scoring, 5 5 5 Truncation is applied to the response string via text.encode("utf-8")[:N].decode("utf-8", errors="ignore") and the truncated string is then re-tokenised for the forward pass. We deliberately do not truncate at token boundaries: a n a_{n} is per-byte, so we need a fixed byte denominator across stages, but tokens-per-byte is tokenizer-dependent and varies across responses with the same byte budget. That variation is harmless because both the bits-numerator and the byte-denominator are computed on the same truncated string. and drop prompts where that common length falls below 50 bytes (150/200 AlpacaEval and 39/100 NB-curated prompts retained; see Section 7 ). We score each (stage, prompt) group with D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} using Qwen2.5-3B as θ \theta and 25 permutations. For comparison we also compute Kirk et al.’s EAD and distinct- n n (averaged over n = 1 ​ … ​ 5 n{=}1\ldots 5 ) and a SentBERT-embedding ( Reimers & Gurevych, 2019 ) similarity-to-diversity reduction.

sections.heading: Hypotheses.
sections.text: We pre-register three one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests ( Dror et al., 2018 ) with family-wise Bonferroni correction across the three contrasts ( Dror et al., 2017 ) ( α = 0.05 / 3 \alpha=0.05/3 ): • H1a D base > D SFT D_{\mathrm{base}}>D_{\mathrm{SFT}} : SFT narrows toward the helpful-assistant style. • H1b D SFT > D DPO D_{\mathrm{SFT}}>D_{\mathrm{DPO}} : DPO is trained on preference data and inherits its typicality bias ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . • H1c D base > D RLVR D_{\mathrm{base}}>D_{\mathrm{RLVR}} : cumulative effect of the full post-training pipeline. The DPO-vs-RLVR comparison is reported as an exploratory two-sided contrast (H1 ′ ): we have no directional prediction for which post-training stage loses more diversity.

sections.heading: Discussion.
sections.text: The monotone drop across all three pre-registered contrasts is consistent with the post-training-reduces-diversity findings of Kirk et al. (2023) ; Padmakumar & He (2023) , now measured by an ICL-based diversity metric that needs neither an embedding model nor a sentence similarity function. Per-prompt D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} also agrees with the lexical (EAD) and semantic (SentBERT) baselines on the same length-matched subset, confirming the metrics see the same diversity-loss signal (Appendix H , Figure 18 ).

sections.heading: Released artefacts.
sections.text: The 200 + \,+\, 100 prompts × \times 4 stages × \times K = 10 K{=}10 generations are released as a public dataset under results/rlhf_experiment/ in the project repository. To our knowledge this is the first public release of K ≥ 10 K\!\geq\!10 sampled responses across a paired SFT/DPO/RL pipeline, filling a gap that blocked direct diversity replication of Kirk et al. (2023) (whose K = 16 K{=}16 generations were not publicly released).

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: We collect the main limitations of the framework and of our D = C × a n D=C\times a_{n} choice in one place so readers can calibrate how strongly to update on the results above. Several points below recap caveats already made in their natural context and cross-reference those for detail.

sections.heading: Measurement is relative to θ \theta ’s perception.
sections.text: The metric evaluates diversity as perceived by the base model θ \theta : if π \pi ’s outputs differ only in ways θ \theta cannot distinguish from context, the metric underestimates diversity (Section 1 , “Important caveat”). Concretely, the off-diagonal sign of the pairwise surprise-reduction matrix changes with θ \theta ’s scale (Section B.4 ), so a k a_{k} curves for the same response set are not directly comparable across different choices of θ \theta .

sections.heading: Metric selection saw the full Tevet benchmark.
sections.text: We chose C × a n C\times a_{n} (rather than alternative summaries such as C × E C\times E ; Appendix D ) after observing its performance on the full Tevet diversity-eval benchmark, without holding out a validation split. The Tevet numbers in Section 5 may therefore be optimistically biased: the scalar form was selected with visibility into those results. The OLMo-2-7B post-training experiment (Section 6 ) was scored after the metric form was fixed and provides independent validation; the synthetic mode-count experiments (Section B.3 ) informally influenced the choice (had they failed, we would likely have revised the metric) and so are not strictly independent.

sections.heading: External benchmark performance trails the strongest baseline.
sections.text: On Tevet and Berant’s diversity-eval benchmark, C × a n C\times a_{n} trails SentBERT by 3.7%–21.0% OCA across the nine binary tasks (Section 5 ); scaling the base model to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) did not close the gap (Appendix G ). We position ICL-based diversity metrics (of which D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} is one instance we found to work well) as a principled complement to embedding-based metrics, not a replacement.

sections.heading: Length-matching drops short-response prompts.
sections.text: Reporting in bits/byte (rather than total bits) makes per-byte cross-entropy not invariant to response length, so the OLMo-2-7B experiment scores a length-matched subset and drops 111 / 300 111/300 prompts whose common per-prompt byte length falls below 50 50 bytes; full mechanics and the un-truncated robustness check are in Section B.6 .

sections.heading: D = C × a n D=C\times a_{n} is a pragmatic choice, not a theoretically derived one.
sections.text: The product form was selected because it captures the properties we wanted a diversity score to have (residual surprise remains after the base model has seen previous responses, low-coherence outputs are penalised, and the result stays on a bits-per-byte scale), not because it is derived from an axiomatic information-theoretic setup. Other scalars respecting the same constraints (weighted integrals of a k − a ∞ a_{k}-a_{\infty} , slope-based scores, or coherence applied at a different point on the curve) could equally be defended (see “The framework admits other metrics” in Section B.6 ). We adopt D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} because it is interpretable and works empirically across our validation regimes, not because it is uniquely correct. We invite other researchers to build on this work to develop other formulas that characterize the a k a_{k} curve in meaningful ways.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We have presented a new approach to measuring diversity using in-context learning, of which D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} is the working instance we evaluate: a base model’s in-context learning detects similarities between arbitrary numbers of responses in a single forward pass. The approach requires no embedding model, no reference corpus, no human labels, and no special-purpose training. The same pipeline scores AI samples and human-written sets. On Tevet and Berant’s human-grounded benchmark it is near the level of the strongest sentence-embedding baseline. On the OLMo-2-7B post-training pipeline it drops across the base → \to SFT → \to DPO/RLVR stages, tracking the diversity loss attributed to RLHF-style training.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This paper presents work which may be used in evaluation pipelines that select for more capable AI systems. We view the prospect of increasingly capable future AI as one of unclear positive or negative net impact. This work may also contribute to the automation of human creative roles. We publish it in the hope that better understanding of machine-generated diversity will contribute to better evaluation and oversight, and that these benefits outweigh the risks.

sections.heading: A.1 Formatting the Conditioning Context
sections.text: Computing θ ⁡ ( r k ∣ r < k , p ) \theta(r_{k}\mid r_{<k},p) requires feeding θ \theta a context containing the prompt and previous responses. The formatting choice affects results, and we use two formats depending on whether the responses are best read as parallel answers to the prompt or as continuations of it. Both are implemented as format_conditioning_context in src/icl_diversity/core.py and selected via a format_mode argument throughout the pipeline.

sections.heading: Instruct format.
sections.text: The default, used for the synthetic scenarios (Appendix B.2 ), the mode-count experiments (Appendix B.3 ), and the OLMo-2-7B post-training case study (Section 6 ): [prompt p] Response A: [r_1] Response B: [r_2] Response C: [r_3] The prompt appears once and each response is introduced by a labelled header (“Response A:”, “Response B:”, …, with labels rolling over to “AA”, “AB” past “Z”), encouraging the base model’s in-context learning to treat the responses as parallel answers to the same prompt.

sections.heading: Completion format.
sections.text: Used for the Tevet and Berant evaluation (Section 5 ), where each response set is a continuation of a shared narrative prompt rather than an instruction-style answer: 1. [prompt p] [r_1] 2. [prompt p] [r_2] 3. [prompt p] [r_3] The prompt is repeated immediately before each response so θ \theta scores r k r_{k} in the same prompt-as-context that produced it. Per-token log-probabilities are extracted only over the response tokens; the bits accumulated over the repeated prompt prefix are excluded from a k a_{k} , keeping the bits-numerator and the per-byte denominator both attributable to r k r_{k} alone.

sections.heading: Base vs. instruction-tuned models.
sections.text: We use a base (non-instruction-tuned) model as θ \theta for two reasons. First, an instruction-tuned model has had its output distribution shaped by RLHF or similar procedures, so using one as θ \theta reintroduces the kind of distributional bias we seek to avoid. Second, an instruction-tuned θ \theta may assign systematically different probabilities to text that follows or violates its alignment training, introducing a confound between coherence-as-fluency and coherence-as-alignment that the metric should not conflate. Modern base models already exhibit strong in-context learning from pretraining alone, so this choice does not sacrifice ICL capability. Optimizing the prompt format to maximally elicit in-context learning from θ \theta is an interesting direction but out of scope for this paper; we use the neutral “Response A/B/C” template throughout.

sections.heading: A.2 Computational Cost
sections.text: Because θ \theta is a causal language model, the full a k a_{k} curve for one response ordering can be computed from a single forward pass . The prompt and all responses are concatenated into one sequence (Figure 3 ). The forward pass produces the log-probability of every token conditioned on all preceding tokens. [prompt p] Response A: [r_1] Response B: [r_2] ... Response N: [r_n] Figure 3 : Single-pass input layout for computing the full a k a_{k} curve. The prompt is followed by all n n responses with “Response A/B/C/…” labels; one forward pass over this sequence yields every a k a_{k} value simultaneously, since causal attention conditions the tokens of r k r_{k} on exactly p , r 1 , … , r k − 1 p,r_{1},\ldots,r_{k-1} (plus formatting). The tokens belonging to r k r_{k} are conditioned on exactly p , r 1 , … , r k − 1 p,r_{1},\ldots,r_{k-1} (plus formatting), which is the conditioning required for a k a_{k} . Partitioning the output log-probabilities by response boundary and summing within each partition yields all n n values of a k a_{k} simultaneously for that ordering, with FLOPs scaling as O ⁡ ( ( | p | + n ​ L ¯ tok ) 2 ) O((|p|+n\bar{L}_{\mathrm{tok}})^{2}) from causal attention, where L ¯ tok \bar{L}_{\mathrm{tok}} is the average response length in tokens. Because we report a ¯ k \bar{a}_{k} averaged over | Σ | |\Sigma| random permutations of the response ordering (Section A.3 ), the total a k a_{k} -curve cost is | Σ | |\Sigma| such passes; the permutations are independent and we batch them on a single GPU. The coherence term C C additionally requires the unconditional per-byte cross-entropies h θ ​ ( r i ∣ p ) h_{\theta}(r_{i}\mid p) for each response. These cannot be extracted from the concatenated pass, since in that pass r i r_{i} for i > 1 i>1 is conditioned on all prior responses. Computing them requires n n independent forward passes, each over the short context ( p , r i ) (p,r_{i}) . These passes are embarrassingly parallel and batchable, and they do not depend on the ordering, so C C is computed once per response set regardless of | Σ | |\Sigma| . In summary, scoring one (prompt, response set) tuple takes: • a k a_{k} curve: | Σ | |\Sigma| forward passes (long context, one per permutation). • C C : n n forward passes (short contexts, batchable; not multiplied by | Σ | |\Sigma| ). With n = 10 n=10 responses and | Σ | = 50 |\Sigma|=50 permutations (our default for larger-scale experiments), this is 50 + 10 = 60 50+10=60 forward passes per (prompt, response set) tuple; the long-context | Σ | |\Sigma| passes dominate wall-clock time.

sections.heading: A.3 Dependence on Sample Ordering
sections.text: The a k a_{k} values depend on the ordering of { r i } \{r_{i}\} . Individual responses differ in how surprising they are to θ \theta given the responses that precede them, so a k a_{k} depends on which response sits at position k k and which others precede it, making a single ordering’s curve jagged. Averaging over random permutations removes this dependence: each position averages over many choices of response and preceding context, so the curve reflects only how θ \theta ’s predictions improve with more context. We therefore average over | Σ | |\Sigma| random permutations; Section B.5 compares low- and high-permutation runs on the validation scenarios and finds that the low setting misranks adjacent scenarios. We have not swept intermediate values and cannot pinpoint a cheap-and-reliable minimum, so we default to | Σ | = 100 |\Sigma|=100 for scenario-level experiments and | Σ | = 50 |\Sigma|=50 elsewhere. Per-response normalization by byte count must be performed before averaging across permutations, since the byte count depends on which response lands at each position. Concretely, the per-byte curve is a mean of per-permutation rates, a ¯ k = 1 | Σ | ​ ∑ σ ∈ Σ a k σ ‖ r σ ⁡ ( k ) ‖ , \bar{a}_{k}=\frac{1}{|\Sigma|}\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\frac{a_{k}^{\sigma}}{\|r_{\sigma(k)}\|}, (6) not a ratio of permutation-averaged bits to permutation-averaged byte counts (which would degenerate, after enough permutations, into the total-bits curve rescaled by the mean response length).

sections.heading: A.4 Choice of n n
sections.text: The diversity score depends on n n as a measurement parameter, not through any estimate of an asymptotic floor. Given enough in-context examples, even genuinely diverse policies eventually become predictable to θ \theta , so a k a_{k} keeps decreasing rather than converging to a meaningful irreducible value: there is no a ∞ a_{\infty} for a n a_{n} to approximate. Too small an n n means θ \theta has not yet exploited the inter-response structure, and D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} overstates diversity. Too large an n n means θ \theta has accumulated enough in-context examples to reduce its surprise even within genuine diversity; for any policy with finitely many distinct modes, a n a_{n} continues to decrease toward zero as θ \theta learns to predict within-mode variation from prior examples. For comparisons to be meaningful, n n must be held fixed across all policies under evaluation. Our experiments use n = 5 n=5 on Tevet (Section 5 ), n = 10 n=10 on OLMo-2-7B and scenario validation, and n = 20 n=20 on the mode-count experiment (Appendix B.3 ). This is one reason to report the full a k a_{k} curve rather than D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} alone. D D is a lossy summary, but the curve shows directly how response surprise evolves at every context size.

sections.heading: B.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We evaluate the metric primarily using Qwen2.5-3B (3B parameters, 32K-token context window) ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , with GPT-2 (124M parameters, 1024-token context window) ( Radford et al., 2019 ) as a smaller-model comparison point for scenario validation. Qwen2.5-3B is used for mode-count scaling, cross-mode learning, and external validation (Sections B.3 , B.4 , 5 ). The cross-model scaling study (Section B.6 ) additionally uses the full Llama 3 family for comparison. All a k a_{k} curves are computed using single-pass forward computation (Section A.2 ). Unless otherwise noted, we use 100 permutations for scenario validation and 50 permutations for larger-scale experiments. Responses are formatted as described in Section A.2 . All code and data, including the Olmo-2 RLHF generations under results/rlhf_experiment/ , are publicly available. 6 6 6 https://github.com/AMindToThink/icl-diversity

sections.heading: B.3 Mode Count Scaling
sections.text: To test whether the metric reflects the number of distinct modes, we construct response sets with m ∈ { 1 , … , 10 } m\in\{1,\ldots,10\} modes drawn from a pool of 50 format-based generators (haiku, code, recipe, legal disclaimer, etc.), all responding to the same prompt (“Write a short piece about rain”). For Qwen2.5-3B: n = 20 n=20 responses, 1000 random draws of mode assignments, averaged over permutations. Figure 5 : Mode count scaling on Qwen2.5-3B ( n = 20 n=20 , 1000 draws). The a k a_{k} curves fan out with increasing m m : higher floors, slower convergence. All curves are exponential (no sigmoidal plateau), even at m = 10 m=10 , due to cross-mode learning (Section B.4 ). Shaded bands around each curve are ± 1 \pm 1 standard error of the mean across the 1000 random draws of mode assignments (i.e., the across-draw standard deviation divided by 1000 \sqrt{1000} ); they are narrow because averaging over 1000 draws sharply reduces the across-draw spread.

sections.heading: Key findings.
sections.text: Figure 5 shows the a k a_{k} curves. a n a_{n} increases monotonically with m m (9.3 bits at m = 1 m=1 to 77.8 bits at m = 10 m=10 ; see Table 6 ), reflecting that with more modes there are fewer same-mode repetitions within n n responses, so each response remains more surprising even after θ \theta has seen the others. This is exactly the behavior D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} needs: a n a_{n} tracks mode count directly. All curves are purely exponential (no sigmoidal plateau), even at m = 10 m=10 ; Section B.4 investigates why. For a detailed comparison of the excess-entropy-based scores on this data, including the sigmoid fit parameters and the non-monotonicity of E ^ n \hat{E}_{n} , see Appendix D .

sections.heading: B.4 Cross-Mode Learning and Curve Shape
sections.text: The authors predicted that at high m m , the a k a_{k} curve should be sigmoidal: an initial plateau (early responses come from different modes and are uninformative about each other), followed by decline once mode repetitions accumulate. GPT-2 shows hints of this pattern at some m m values (e.g. m = 10 m=10 ). Qwen2.5-3B does not: it shows immediate exponential decay at all m m . This section investigates the discrepancy through systematic pairwise analysis.

sections.heading: Pairwise cross-mode surprise matrix.
sections.text: For 15 modes, we compute a 15 × 15 15\times 15 matrix M i ​ j M_{ij} : the surprise reduction (in bits) when a response from mode j j is in the context and mode i i is the target. Diagonal entries measure same-mode learning; off-diagonal entries measure cross-mode information transfer. Each entry averages over 5 context–target samples (using different samples for context and target to avoid self-prediction inflation). (a) Qwen2.5-3B: positive off-diagonal. (b) GPT-2: negative off-diagonal. Figure 6 : Pairwise cross-mode surprise reduction matrices. Each cell ( i , j ) (i,j) shows how many bits of surprise reduction mode i i (target) receives from seeing mode j j (context). Qwen shows diagonal dominance with pervasive positive off-diagonal (+1.9 bits mean); GPT-2 shows diagonal dominance with negative off-diagonal (-3.7 bits mean).

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: (Cell standard deviations are the mean within-cell sampling std across the 15 diagonal or 210 off-diagonal matrix cells, each estimated from 5 context-target sample pairs.) • Qwen2.5-3B : diagonal mean = 60.5 ± 14.4 60.5\pm 14.4 bits, off-diagonal mean = + 1.9 ± 2.5 +1.9\pm 2.5 bits, 64% of off-diagonal entries positive. • GPT-2 : diagonal mean = 83.0 ± 20.0 83.0\pm 20.0 bits, off-diagonal mean = − 3.7 -3.7 bits, only 30% of off-diagonal entries positive. The sign of the off-diagonal determines the curve shape (Figure 6 ): • Positive off-diagonal (Qwen) : Every response in context lowers expected surprise on every other response. The a k a_{k} curve drops from position 1, producing exponential decay. • Negative off-diagonal (GPT-2) : Cross-mode responses actively raise surprise on subsequent responses. At m = 10 m=10 , the expected first-step net drop under the additive independent-mode model is only + 4.9 +4.9 bits (the 8.3-bit diagonal gain from the 1 / m 1/m same-mode chance is largely offset by the − 3.4 -3.4 -bit cross-mode damage from the ( m − 1 ) / m (m{-}1)/m different-mode chance), producing a flat plateau until same-mode repetitions accumulate, the predicted sigmoid. GPT-2 has a larger diagonal and a negative off-diagonal: it gains more from same-mode context but is actively penalised by cross-mode context. The two effects are linked, since probability mass that conditioning concentrates on same-mode continuations is mass taken away from other modes; a sharper conditional on the seen mode is necessarily worse on the unseen ones. Qwen does the opposite: a smaller diagonal but a positive off-diagonal, distributing its update across modes.

sections.heading: Pairwise asymmetry.
sections.text: The mean absolute asymmetry | M i ​ j − M j ​ i | |M_{ij}-M_{ji}| is 5.6 bits ( 3.0 × 3.0\times the off-diagonal mean), falsifying the hypothesis that pairwise surprise reduction is symmetric (Figure 7 ). Information-theoretically I ⁡ ( X , Y ) = I ⁡ ( Y , X ) I(X;Y)=I(Y;X) , so this asymmetry cannot reflect asymmetric information structure between modes; it reflects θ \theta ’s imperfection as an in-context reasoner. The same content is more useful as context than as target depending on its surface form, mirroring the reversal curse observed in autoregressive LLMs trained on “A is B” but failing on “B is A” ( Berglund et al., 2023 ) . Figure 7 : Pairwise symmetry scatter for Qwen2.5-3B: each point is one ( i , j ) (i,j) pair, plotting M i ​ j M_{ij} vs. M j ​ i M_{ji} . Under symmetric mutual information, points would lie on y = x y=x . The best-fit slope is 0.46 ( R 2 = 0.24 R^{2}=0.24 ), and many pairs have opposite signs: mode i i can reduce surprise for mode j j while j j increases surprise for i i .

sections.heading: Connections to information-theoretic properties.
sections.text: Two information-theoretic properties are relevant to interpreting the pairwise matrix: 1. Non-negative conditioning ( H ⁡ ( X ) ≥ H ⁡ ( X ∣ Y ) H(X)\geq H(X\mid Y) ): Under the true distribution, conditioning can never increase entropy on average. For cross-entropies this is not guaranteed (the KL term can increase), but a well-calibrated θ \theta should show mostly non-negative off-diagonal entries. 2. Symmetry of mutual information ( I ⁡ ( X , Y ) = I ⁡ ( Y , X ) I(X;Y)=I(Y;X) ): Under the true joint, row means (how informative mode i i is as context) should correlate with column means (how much mode i i benefits from context). (a) Qwen2.5-3B: slope = 0.84, R 2 = 0.34 R^{2}=0.34 . (b) GPT-2: slope = 0.35, R 2 = 0.08 R^{2}=0.08 . Figure 8 : Row mean (how informative as context) vs. column mean (how much benefit from context) for each mode. Qwen shows tighter correlation closer to the identity, consistent with approximate symmetry of mutual information. GPT-2 shows widespread violations of non-negative conditioning (modes in the negative-row-mean region). Figure 8 compares the two models. Qwen shows a tighter row–column relationship (slope = 0.84, R 2 = 0.34 R^{2}=0.34 ) with only 1 of 15 modes having a negative column mean. GPT-2 shows widespread violations of non-negative conditioning (6 modes with negative column means) and a barely-existent row–column relationship (slope = 0.35, R 2 = 0.08 R^{2}=0.08 ). Across the four Llama models ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Meta AI, 2024 ) we additionally tested (Section B.6 , Figure 10 ), the fraction of positive off-diagonal entries rises monotonically with size (25% at 1B to 63% at 70B), and the off-diagonal mean follows the same trend (-4.9 bits at 1B to +2.1 bits at 70B): the magnitude of cross-mode information transfer increases with size. The row–column relationship does not: R 2 R^{2} peaks at Llama-3B (0.67) and degrades at the larger Llamas (0.09 at 70B), so the symmetry of the pairwise matrix does not correspondingly improve.

sections.heading: Discussion.
sections.text: The paper’s sigmoid prediction assumes modes are approximately independent. For capable models, this fails: cross-mode learning creates positive information transfer between distinct modes. The Llama 1B/3B/8B/70B series confirms this scales with model size (Section B.6 ): the total cross-mode information θ \theta extracts grows monotonically with size, and with it non-negative conditioning is better satisfied. The matrix nevertheless remains asymmetric (row–column R 2 R^{2} peaks at Llama-3B and degrades at the larger Llamas), which under I ⁡ ( X , Y ) = I ⁡ ( Y , X ) I(X;Y)=I(Y;X) signals that even Llama-70B is an imperfect in-context reasoner.

sections.heading: Permutation sensitivity.
sections.text: The per-byte a k a_{k} curve depends on the response ordering. Comparing the D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} ranking of the 5 validation scenarios from Section B.2 between 3- and 100-permutation runs: on GPT-2, 2 of 5 scenarios shift rank between the two settings; on Qwen2.5-3B, 2 of 5. Where scenarios do shift rank, it is between adjacent scenarios with similar D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} values rather than dramatic reorderings. We use 100 permutations throughout for scenario-level experiments; we have not swept intermediate values, so we cannot pinpoint a minimum that is both cheap and reliable. The coherence term C C is permutation-invariant by construction and unaffected.

sections.heading: Boundary handling.
sections.text:
When Qwen merges a response’s final . with the following 

 into a single .

 token, our boundary detector (which uses a character-span overlap rule) attributes that token to the response, not the separator. The response’s cross-entropy therefore includes a small contribution from predicting the upcoming separator alongside its own characters; the byte-count denominator remains the response’s literal byte length. We have not measured the magnitude of this bias on our reported numbers. Boundary correctness is verified by tests/test_response_boundaries.py .

sections.heading: σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} is a diagnostic, not a diversity signal.
sections.text: σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} increased monotonically with m m in our synthetic experiments because our modes have very different formats (code vs. haiku vs. recipe → \to different per-byte cross-entropies). But σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} measures coherence heterogeneity , not diversity: modes with similar fluency would have low σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} despite high diversity, and a single mode with high quality variance could have high σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} with zero diversity. Its role is diagnostic (detecting mixed coherence), not as a standalone diversity score.

sections.heading: Cross-mode information scales with model quality.
sections.text: We test how cross-mode information transfer varies with θ \theta ’s scale by running the pairwise matrix experiment on 4 dense Llama models (1B, 3B, 8B, 70B) using the same 15 modes and 5 samples per mode. Figure 10 shows the results. The off-diagonal mean increases monotonically with model size: − 4.9 -4.9 (1B), − 1.4 -1.4 (3B), − 1.2 -1.2 (8B), + 2.1 +2.1 (70B) bits, transitioning from negative (cross-mode context hurts) to positive (cross-mode context helps). The fraction of positive off-diagonal entries follows the same monotone trend: 25%, 41%, 44%, 63%. This hypothesis was pre-registered before running any Llama models, and the probability of accidental monotonicity across 4 models under the null is 1 / 4 ! ≈ 4.2 % 1/4!\approx 4.2\% . sections.heading: The framework admits other metrics.
sections.text: The a k a_{k} curve is the primary object of our framework, and D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} is one natural summary of it among many. Reporting the curve directly preserves information that any single scalar (including ours) collapses. Alternative scalars could be derived from the same curve to capture different desiderata: weighted sums of a k − a ∞ a_{k}-a_{\infty} (emphasizing early or late positions), the slope or curvature at a specific k k (measuring how quickly θ \theta learns), curve-shape descriptors, or coherence-weighted variants that combine C C with quantities other than a n a_{n} . Different applications may warrant different choices; for instance, a policy-comparison setting might prefer a metric sensitive to changes in the curve shape, while a ranking setting needs a single well-behaved scalar. We have not explored this space systematically; we focus on D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} because it empirically works well across regimes and has a clean information-theoretic interpretation, but we expect the framework to support a family of related metrics with complementary properties. One untested family is coherence-reweighting: a practitioner with a clear preference for sharper Mixed penalisation could replace C × a n C\times a_{n} with C α × a n C^{\alpha}\times a_{n} for α > 1 \alpha>1 to drive low-coherence sets toward zero faster. We have not evaluated such variants on the Tevet or OLMo experiments and so make no empirical claim about them.

sections.heading: Bits/byte vs. total bits, and the length-matching consequence.
sections.text: A separate choice within the framework is whether to report total bits (length-dependent but tokenizer-agnostic) or per-byte bits/byte (also tokenizer-agnostic, with length scaled out). We default to bits/byte for the headline diversity score, but per-byte quantities are not invariant to response length: in a causal LM, longer responses give θ \theta more within-response context to predict later tokens, lowering per-byte surprise. For the OLMo-2-7B experiment (Section 6 ) raw response length is not monotone across stages, so we score the length-matched subset as the headline analysis: every response in a (stage, prompt) tuple is truncated to a common per-prompt UTF-8 byte length (the minimum across all 40 responses) before scoring. 111 / 300 111/300 prompts had a per-prompt common length below 50 bytes – driven by the base model on AlpacaEval (no instruction-following prior) and by SFT on NB-curated short-answer prompts – and were dropped because length-matching them would compare essentially-empty fragments. The headline numbers therefore condition on the 150 / 200 150/200 AlpacaEval and 39 / 100 39/100 NB-curated prompts where length-matching is well-defined; the dropped prompts are themselves a stage-specific behavioural signal we are not measuring here. We also verified that the monotone D D drop holds on the un-truncated 200 + 100 200+100 prompt sets, with all three pre-registered H1 contrasts remaining Bonferroni-significant at p < 10 − 13 p<10^{-13} on both prompt sets. Full numbers and reproduction commands are in investigations/length_matched_rlhf/VERDICT.md .

sections.heading: Appendix C Future Work
sections.text: Several directions remain unexplored.

sections.heading: Prompt format optimization.
sections.text: We use a fixed prompt template throughout and do not attempt to optimize it for ICL elicitation. Prompt engineering could improve the metric’s discriminative power. Dimension-specific framings (e.g., “Here are several stories in different genres”) are one such variant: priming θ \theta to expect variation along a dimension removes the small portion of the surprise attributable to the mere existence of that variation, but it does not isolate per-dimension diversity, since the rest of the cross-response surprise reduction remains.

sections.heading: Ensembling base models.
sections.text: A single base model θ \theta may produce non-monotone a k a_{k} curves when pushed out of distribution by long contexts. Ensembling multiple base models at the token level (averaging softmax probabilities) could stabilize the estimates while preserving the autoregressive structure. Our codebase supports token-level ensembling, but we have not yet validated it experimentally.

sections.heading: Disagreement cases with other metrics.
sections.text: We report aggregate correlations with embedding-based and reference metrics on Tevet’s tasks (Section 5 ) but do not look at which response sets the metrics rank differently. Identifying prompts or response sets where C × a n C\times a_{n} disagrees with SentBERT, distinct- n n , or McDiv is the most direct way to characterise what each metric is actually measuring; the disagreements are where the choice of metric matters. We expect two regimes to drive disagreement: response sets that share arbitrary rare patterns a base model can pick up on but that fall outside what a fixed sentence embedder represents (where C × a n C\times a_{n} should detect repetition that embeddings miss), and response sets where one response is a mixture of two others (where progressive conditioning credits the mixture for being predictable from its components, while pairwise embedding-distance averages do not).

sections.heading: Total-bits variants of D D .
sections.text: We report D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} in bits/byte for length control, normalising by bytes rather than tokens so that scores remain tokenizer-agnostic. The implementation also exposes a n a_{n} in total bits, which is likewise tokenizer-agnostic but not length-controlled. A hybrid scalar C × a n bits C\times a_{n}^{\text{bits}} rewards length (longer responses have more positions at which to be surprising), which some practitioners may want; characterising when each variant is the appropriate measurement target is left to future work.

sections.heading: Optimizing generators against D D .
sections.text: We use C × a n C\times a_{n} as an evaluation-time diagnostic, but it could in principle serve as a training or decoding objective. Future work could fine-tune or sample from a generator π \pi with the goal of maximizing C × a n C\times a_{n} under a fixed base model θ \theta to push π \pi toward response sets that are both coherent and diverse.

sections.heading: Appendix D Excess Entropy and the C × E C\times E Score
sections.text: This appendix develops the excess entropy E E , an alternative summary of the a k a_{k} curve that is theoretically interesting (connecting to the excess entropy of computational mechanics ( Crutchfield & Feldman, 2003 ) and to the total correlation) but empirically inferior to D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} on the external benchmarks of Section 5 . We tried both the last-point estimator E ^ n \hat{E}_{n} and a sigmoid-extrapolated projected floor for a ∞ a_{\infty} (Section D.1 ); we stopped using E E when it became clear it cannot distinguish diverse from non-diverse response sets in the few-draws regime where modes do not repeat within n n samples. We include it here for theoretical completeness, as a null result, and to explain the empirical comparisons that motivate our preference for D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} .

sections.heading: D.1 The Excess Entropy
sections.text: The primary metric D C ​ a n = C × a n D_{Ca_{n}}=C\times a_{n} uses the curve’s endpoint a n a_{n} : as the surprise after conditioning on n − 1 n-1 peer responses, a n a_{n} reflects both the curve’s level and the drop from a 1 a_{1} in a single scalar. Section 5 shows this combination is what discriminates diverse from non-diverse response sets in the few-draws regime, while a 1 a_{1} alone (the level) and E E (the integrated drop, defined below) each underperform. We thought that E E ’s learnable structure would be interesting and track diversity. Following the concept of excess entropy from computational mechanics ( Crutchfield & Feldman, 2003 ) , define the excess entropy : E = ∑ k = 1 ∞ ( a k − a ∞ ) E=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(a_{k}-a_{\infty}\bigr) (7) Units: bits. This is the total learnable structural information in the progressive conditioning process, above the irreducible residual noise. It converges whenever θ \theta ’s surprise at new responses eventually stabilizes (since a k → a ∞ a_{k}\to a_{\infty} and the excess e k = a k − a ∞ e_{k}=a_{k}-a_{\infty} decays to zero). The “structure” captured by E E is not limited to discrete mode identity: it includes any inter-response regularity to which θ \theta assigns lower conditional surprise. In practice, a ∞ a_{\infty} is unknown. We estimate it as a n a_{n} (the last observed value) and compute: E ^ n = ∑ k = 1 n ( a k − a n ) \hat{E}_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(a_{k}-a_{n}) (8) This underestimates E E (since a n ≥ a ∞ a_{n}\geq a_{\infty} ), but the bias decreases with n n .

sections.heading: Parametric extrapolation of a ∞ a_{\infty} .
sections.text: Rather than using a n a_{n} directly, one can fit a parametric model to the observed curve and extrapolate a ∞ a_{\infty} . The a k a_{k} curve is theoretically expected to be sigmoidal (with concave-up/exponential decay as the degenerate case when the inflection point k 0 < 1 k_{0}<1 ). This motivates fitting a four-parameter sigmoid: a k = a ∞ + α 1 + e β ⁡ ( k − k 0 ) a_{k}=a_{\infty}+\frac{\alpha}{1+e^{\beta(k-k_{0})}} (9) where a ∞ a_{\infty} is the asymptotic floor, α \alpha is the total drop from a 1 a_{1} to a ∞ a_{\infty} , β > 0 \beta>0 controls the steepness of the transition, and k 0 k_{0} is the inflection point. The fit yields a ∞ a_{\infty} without requiring n n to be large enough for convergence. Section B.3 provides empirical evidence that the sigmoid-extrapolated E fit E_{\mathrm{fit}} recovers the expected monotonic relationship between mode count and excess entropy, while the raw E ^ n \hat{E}_{n} estimator does not.

sections.text: The excess entropy E = ∑ k ( a k − a ∞ ) E=\sum_{k}(a_{k}-a_{\infty}) is in bits. For a length-normalized variant, we define the per-byte excess entropy rate by normalizing each response’s surprise by its byte count before averaging across permutations. For a single permutation σ \sigma , the per-byte conditional surprise at position k k is a k σ / ‖ r σ ⁡ ( k ) ‖ a_{k}^{\sigma}/\|r_{\sigma(k)}\| (bits/byte). Averaging over permutations gives a ^ k rate = 𝔼 σ ​ [ a k σ ‖ r σ ⁡ ( k ) ‖ ] \hat{a}_{k}^{\mathrm{rate}}=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\!\left[\frac{a_{k}^{\sigma}}{\|r_{\sigma(k)}\|}\right] (11) and the per-byte floor is estimated analogously from the last position: a ^ ∞ rate = a ^ n rate \hat{a}_{\infty}^{\mathrm{rate}}=\hat{a}_{n}^{\mathrm{rate}} . The per-byte excess entropy rate is E rate = ∑ k = 1 n ( a ^ k rate − a ^ ∞ rate ) . E_{\mathrm{rate}}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(\hat{a}_{k}^{\mathrm{rate}}-\hat{a}_{\infty}^{\mathrm{rate}}\bigr). (12) This treats each response equally regardless of length. Note that E rate ≠ E / B ¯ E_{\mathrm{rate}}\neq E/\bar{B} in general: because total surprise a k a_{k} and byte count ‖ r k ‖ \|r_{k}\| are positively correlated, E / B ¯ E/\bar{B} overweights long responses, while the per-response normalization in E rate E_{\mathrm{rate}} avoids this.

sections.heading: D.4 Why Not Weight Excess Entropy Inside the Sum?
sections.text: A natural alternative to reporting E E and C C separately is to weight the terms within E E by coherence, computing E w = ∑ k w k ⋅ ( a k − a ∞ ) E_{w}=\sum_{k}w_{k}\cdot(a_{k}-a_{\infty}) where w k = 2 − h θ ​ ( r k ∣ p ) w_{k}=2^{-h_{\theta}(r_{k}\mid p)} . This would suppress contributions from incoherent modes directly at the point of measurement. We considered and rejected this approach because it breaks the information-theoretic interpretation. E = ∑ k e k E=\sum_{k}e_{k} has a clean meaning as the total structural information above the noise floor, connected to Crutchfield and Feldman’s excess entropy, and inserting weights makes E w E_{w} a hybrid quantity that is not the excess entropy of any well-defined process.

sections.heading: D.5 Limitations of C × E C\times E
sections.text: C × E C\times E inherits two limitations from E E . First, E E measures recurrence : surprise reduction as multiple responses accumulate, rather than continuous spread. A policy that draws from a broad, roughly continuous distribution of coherent outputs has a k ≈ a 1 a_{k}\approx a_{1} for all k k , yielding E ≈ 0 E\approx 0 despite maximal diversity. Second, E E is near-zero in the few-draws regime: with only 5–10 responses and no repeated modes, θ \theta finds little learnable structure regardless of diversity, so C × E C\times E carries almost no signal. These limitations are the reason D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} is preferred as the primary score: a ∞ a_{\infty} is the level of the floor, which differs meaningfully between diverse and non-diverse response sets even when the curve stays nearly flat.

sections.heading: Why E E fails in this regime.
sections.text: With only 5 responses and no repeated modes, θ \theta finds little learnable structure regardless of diversity. The a k a_{k} curve stays approximately flat, yielding E ≈ 0 E\approx 0 for both diverse and non-diverse sets. The E E -based scores thus carry almost no signal. The asymptotic floor a ∞ a_{\infty} , by contrast, differs substantially between the two conditions: diverse responses remain surprising after conditioning ( a ∞ a_{\infty} high), while paraphrases become predictable ( a ∞ a_{\infty} low). This is the fundamental reason D C ​ a n D_{Ca_{n}} is preferred.

sections.heading: Appendix E Dataset Construction Confounds in McDiv
sections.text: When validating against the McDiv_nuggets benchmark ( Tevet & Berant, 2021 ) , we observed that the mean a ¯ 1 \bar{a}_{1} curve (per-byte) for the “low diversity” group starts above the “high diversity” group in the story_gen task (Figure 15 ). Since a 1 a_{1} measures the surprise of the first response conditioned only on the prompt (before any other responses appear in context), this gap cannot reflect diversity. It is a confound in the dataset construction.

sections.heading: E.1 Mechanism
sections.text: The McDiv protocol (Tevet and Berant §6.4), from which McDiv_nuggets is sampled (Tevet and Berant Appendix C.2 specifies McDiv_nuggets as the 3K subset of McDiv on which distinct- n n correlates at zero), pairs a low-diversity set with each high-diversity set as follows. Workers first write five different continuations (the high-diversity set). The same worker is then asked to self-select one of their own five responses and paraphrase it five times, preserving content while varying form (the low-diversity set). Tevet and Berant do not characterize the distribution of which responses workers self-select. Empirically (see Table 7 and Figure 15 , and the illustrative examples from the McDiv_nuggets story_gen dataset in Section E.3 below), we observe that the self-selected endings for the low-diversity sets tend to be more specific or dramatic (e.g., “He scored winner” or “they quit”) than the typical high-diversity continuations (e.g., “Joel fired the cook when things went too far downhill”). This means that individual low-diversity responses are intrinsically more surprising to the base model, not because of diversity, but because of the specificity of the endings workers self-selected for paraphrasing.

sections.heading: E.4 Implications
sections.text: The construction confound (low-diversity sets are paraphrases of specific dramatic endings rather than a random subsample of low-diversity content) lifts the entire a ¯ k \bar{a}_{k} curve on low-diversity sets, since their content is intrinsically surprising under θ \theta at every k k , and pushes C C down because the same content is less coherent. a 1 a_{1} ’s upward shift opposes the diversity label; C C ’s downward shift happens to align with it (a confound artifact, not coherence genuinely tracking diversity). At a n a_{n} , the diversity signal we are measuring overrides the confound’s upward pull: paraphrases collapse to predictable once θ \theta has seen the others while genuinely diverse responses do not, so a n a_{n} ends up lower on low-diversity sets and C × a n C\times a_{n} tracks the label despite the confound (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: Appendix F Aggregation Across Prompts
sections.text: This appendix concerns aggregation across prompts. Aggregation within a single prompt, across permutations of the response ordering, is described in Section A.3 and given by Eq. ( 6 ): the per-byte a ¯ k \bar{a}_{k} is a mean of per-permutation per-byte rates, not a ratio of permutation-averaged bits to permutation-averaged byte counts. 7 7 7 An earlier revision of our implementation computed the ratio-of-means form, in which the bits and byte counts at each position are each averaged across permutations before dividing. After enough permutations, the byte counts at each position approach the mean response length, so that estimator collapses into the total-bits curve rescaled by a single constant, losing the per-permutation per-byte signal that Eq. To summarize a policy’s diversity across a prompt suite P = { p 1 , … , p M } P=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{M}\} , one can average: D ¯ C ​ a n ​ ( π ) = 1 M ​ ∑ j = 1 M D C ​ a n ​ ( π , p j ) \bar{D}_{Ca_{n}}(\pi)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}D_{Ca_{n}}(\pi,p_{j}) (14) To compare two policies π 1 \pi_{1} and π 2 \pi_{2} , the natural scalar is the difference: Δ ​ D C ​ a n = D ¯ C ​ a n ​ ( π 1 ) − D ¯ C ​ a n ​ ( π 2 ) \Delta D_{Ca_{n}}=\bar{D}_{Ca_{n}}(\pi_{1})-\bar{D}_{Ca_{n}}(\pi_{2}) (15) Δ ​ D C ​ a n \Delta D_{Ca_{n}} answers “how much more plausibility-weighted residual diversity does π 1 \pi_{1} have than π 2 \pi_{2} , on average across prompts?” No division is involved, so Δ ​ D C ​ a n \Delta D_{Ca_{n}} is stable even when either policy’s score is near zero.

sections.heading: Result: scaling did not help on the binary tasks.
sections.text: On the 12 binary classification tasks (McDiv, McDiv_nuggets, ConTest), Qwen2.5-3B wins on 11 of 12, with ConTest prompt_gen the only marginal win for Qwen3-30B-A3B ( + 0.005 +0.005 AUC). sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: The binary result is a clear negative: scaling from 3B to 30B active parameters does not improve discrimination on McDiv or ConTest. We do not have a confident explanation. The Qwen3-30B-A3B run was not repeated after a bug fix applied to the primary experiments, so the comparison should be treated as preliminary. We leave the question of whether larger base models improve the metric on binary tasks to future work.
